notes.meaning: King Darius organized his newly conquered kingdom by setting one hundred and twenty regional leaders over the provinces. These officials, called satraps, were placed throughout the empire to keep order and administer the king's rule. This setup provided stable government across a vast and diverse territory.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many historical critics argue that Darius the Mede is unknown in outside ancient records and view the reference as a historical mistake, whereas conservative scholars identify him with the governor Gubaru, Cambyses, or Cyrus himself.

notes.meaning: The king appointed three top administrators to supervise all the satraps, and Daniel was selected as one of the three. Their job was to audit the provincial books so the king would suffer no loss through theft or fraud. Even in advanced old age, Daniel was trusted with great civil power.

Daniel quickly stood out above the other administrators and leaders because he possessed an extraordinary spirit of wisdom and honesty. Seeing his exceptional skill and good character, King Darius planned to place him over the entire realm as prime minister. God blessed Daniel with favor even under a foreign ruler.

The other administrators and satraps grew deeply jealous and tried to dig up corruption or mistakes in Daniel's government work. They searched thoroughly but could find no dishonesty, negligence, or scandal anywhere in his record because he was entirely trustworthy. When believers live faithfully, their integrity silences their critics.

Recognizing that Daniel's public record was spotless, the conspirators realized they could only trap him through his religious devotion. They decided to create a conflict between the civil law of the kingdom and the law of Daniel's God. His steadfast piety was the only target they could attack.

The plotting officials gathered into an eager group and approached the king with great flattery. They offered the customary court greeting wishing that the king might live forever. Their noisy, united appearance gave an impression of loyal urgency while hiding a deadly scheme.

The officials falsely claimed that all the imperial leaders had agreed to propose a special royal decree. For thirty days, no one in the kingdom would be allowed to pray to any god or make a request of any man except King Darius, on penalty of being thrown to the lions. This played directly to the king's pride while setting an unavoidable trap for Daniel.

The conspirators urged the king to sign the written order immediately to make it binding and irrevocable. Under the constitution of the Medes and Persians, once a royal decree was officially signed, it could never be cancelled or altered. This legal rule guaranteed that the king could not later pardon Daniel.

Deceived by the cunning flatterers and pleased with the idea of testing his subjects' loyalty, Darius signed the document into law. He failed to see the malice behind the proposal and acted without careful thought. Rulers often fall into foolish mistakes when they accept unearned praise.

As soon as Daniel learned that the decree had been signed, he went straight home to pray. He opened the windows of his upstairs room toward Jerusalem and got down on his knees three times a day to pray and give thanks to God, just as he had always done. True devotion does not retreat or compromise when faith is made a crime.

differ.view: Some highlight that Daniel engaged in open civil disobedience based on personal conviction and conscience, noting that while Scripture requires prayer, the specific practice of praying at an open window three times daily was not an explicit biblical mandate.

notes.meaning: The conspirators rushed to Daniel's house in a crowd, expecting to catch him in the act. They found him on his knees, openly praying and asking his God for grace. Daniel's steady obedience gave them the exact evidence they needed to carry out their scheme.

The men went straight to the king and first asked him to confirm his decree about the thirty-day ban on prayer. Once Darius reaffirmed that the order stood firm under the unchangeable law of the Medes and Persians, their legal trap was sprung. They secured the king's public word before ever mentioning Daniel's name.

The accusers then denounced Daniel, describing him dismissively as a Jewish exile rather than an honored high official. They charged him with showing complete disregard for the king and his royal decree by praying to his God three times each day. They twisted his quiet devotion into political rebellion.

Hearing Daniel's name, the king was crushed with grief and deeply displeased with himself for being so easily tricked. He valued Daniel greatly and spent the rest of the day until sunset working to find a legal way to rescue him. Foolish promises made in haste often lead to painful regret.

At sunset, the conspirators returned together to press the king to execute the sentence. They reminded him that under Persian law, no king could reverse or dispense with an official decree that had been signed. They used the rigid legal system to block any royal mercy.

Helpless against the pressure of his lords, Darius gave the command, and Daniel was thrown into the lions' pit. As Daniel was cast in, the king offered a hopeful parting word, saying that the God Daniel served continually would surely deliver him. Even a pagan ruler recognized Daniel's steady, lifelong faithfulness.

A heavy stone was placed over the mouth of the pit, and the king sealed it with his signet ring and the rings of his nobles. This ensured that no one could rescue Daniel secretly, and the nobles could not harm him if the lions did not. God turned this human security into undeniable proof of a miraculous rescue.

King Darius went back to his palace and spent a miserable, sleepless night fasting. He refused any food, company, or musical entertainment because his conscience troubled him so deeply. Earthly splendor brings no peace to a soul burdened by its own wrongdoing.

At the very first sign of daybreak, the king rose from his bed and hurried out to the lions' den. His deep concern for Daniel drove him past the fear of what his nobles might think. He could not wait even for normal daylight to discover Daniel's fate.

As he drew near the pit, the king called out with an anxious, grieving voice to see if Daniel was alive. He addressed Daniel as the servant of the living God and asked whether his God had been able to save him from the lions. Darius had a faint, trembling hope, but Daniel possessed true peace.

Daniel answered from the pit, greeting the monarch respectfully with the wish that the king might live forever. He showed no bitterness or anger toward Darius for handing him over to death. Believers can show genuine kindness to earthly leaders even when suffering mistreatment.

Daniel announced that God had sent His angel to shut the lions' mouths so they could not hurt him at all. He explained that he was preserved because he was innocent before God, and he had committed no crime against the king by remaining true to his prayers. Obeying God first is never an act of treason against rightful authority.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic expositors have cited Daniel's declared innocence as an example of God rewarding human uprightness and good works, while Protestant commentators respond that Daniel claimed blamelessness only concerning the specific charge of wrongdoing against the king.

notes.meaning: The king was overjoyed and immediately commanded that Daniel be lifted up out of the den. When Daniel was brought out, they found not a single scratch or wound on his body because he had trusted in his God. True faith rests entirely in God's keeping, whatever the earthly outcome may be.

By order of the king, the men who had plotted Daniel's death were cast into the lions' den along with their families, following harsh Persian custom. The hungry lions attacked them instantly and broke their bones before they even hit the floor of the pit. This terrible end confirmed the miracle by showing how ferocious the beasts really were.

King Darius sent a royal proclamation to all peoples, nations, and language groups throughout his whole realm. He began his letter with a traditional wish that their peace and well-being might increase. His goal was to make the wonder of Daniel's deliverance known to the entire empire.

The king commanded everyone across his territories to revere and stand in awe of the God of Daniel. He proclaimed that this God is the living God who endures forever, whose kingdom cannot be destroyed, and whose rule has no end. The rescue of one faithful servant moved a great empire to acknowledge God's majesty.

Darius praised God as the great Deliverer who rescues His people and performs signs and wonders in both heaven and earth. He pointed to Daniel's survival in the lions' den as living proof of God's unmatched saving power. God turns the trials of His people into public testimonies of His glory.

Daniel continued to thrive and hold honorable office throughout the reign of Darius and on into the reign of Cyrus the Persian. God guarded His servant through several regime changes, preserving him to help his exiled people. Steadfast loyalty to the Lord outlasts every earthly empire.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read the phrase 'reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus' as referring to two consecutive or overlapping kings, while others interpret the phrase as 'the reign of Darius, even the reign of Cyrus,' viewing Darius as an alternate title for Cyrus himself.
